text:
Residents of Iowa, Illinois and Missouri who are preparing for Thanksgiving are also bracing themselves for the detonation of hazardous bomb-making materials, after the US army announced it would go through with plans for a controlled explosion on Wednesday.
The detonation of 68 barrels of lead azide is now scheduled for 10am EST after being delayed several times over the past week amid public outcry and political wrangling.
In a press conference, officials said they were not able to find a “viable alternative” after the material, which is stored at an ammunition plant in Middletown, Iowa, was discovered to be dangerously unstable earlier this year.
“There is consensus across experts across the country that a controlled, mitigated detonation of the lead azide here at Iowa Army Ammunition Plant is far preferable to an uncontrolled, spontaneous detonation of that substance,” said Adam Telle, acting secretary of the US Army.
The operation was initially planned for last Friday, but was rescheduled three times as public concern grew and environmentalists sued to block the detonation. Donald Trump ordered the military to hold off on detonation pending a court ruling and a sign-off from the Democratic governor-elect, Rob Sand, who does not take office until January.
The chaotic back-and-forth has left many locals confused and frustrated as they attempt to keep up with shifting closures of schools and businesses and unclear toxin mitigation recommendations. While residents of Middletown have been aware of the plans since at least a month ago when a public meeting was held on the topic, neighboring communities were not informed until the army publicly announced plans on 15 November, five days before the initially scheduled detonation. Politicians, including Iowa governor Kim Reynolds, stated they were also first briefed that day.
The explosion risks releasing plumes of toxic chemicals in a 100-mile (160km) radius, but exactly where those toxins will land has changed with each rescheduled date. Residents within five miles of the detonation are being encouraged to evacuate, and those within the immediate 20-mile radius are being advised to stay indoors with windows closed to avoid airbound dust.
The Iowa department of health and human services has recommended that residents of affected areas stay indoors for 24-48 hours of the blast, an advisory that is at odds with scheduling the day before Thanksgiving, one of the heaviest travel days of the year.
Muscatine, a town approximately 60 miles north of Middletown along the Mississippi River, was initially placed in the path of the plume by prediction models. Rehana Pasha, an employee at farm supply chain Blain’s Farm & Fleet, said she had been fielding questions from concerned farmers since the plans were first announced last week. She said supplies like containers to safely store water, tarps to cover livestock feed, and leaf-blowers to blow lead dust and other contaminants off surfaces had been selling fast.
“Initially we had only five days of warning, and as a farm supply store we were overwhelmed with customers asking how to prepare,” she said, adding that their customer base skews older and was struggling to order supplies on Amazon and other e-commerce sites on such short notice.
The most recent blast models predict the plume will head south-west into southern Iowa and Missouri, where officials say approximately 350 farms could be affected. At Tuesday’s press conference, USDA official Richard Fordyce said federal agencies “have proper protocols in place to ensure there are no heavy metals, including lead, in the food that enters the supply chain”.
Some farmers are already taking such measures into their own hands, said Brandon Hanson, whose livestock and animal feed company Hanson Farms distributed more than 100 free lead-testing kits before the detonation. The business is encouraging customers to test their soil before and after the blast to monitor any changes and protect their livestock. He said the abruptly rescheduled detonation left many locals frustrated.
“They’re upset because they had made plans – they had taped windows, come up with different locations for their animals, and dumped out water for the night just to find out that it wasn’t going to happen,” he said. “Living nearby, I am concerned about waking up in the middle of the night and it having already exploded in my backyard.”
The saga has raised questions about the mismanagement of the explosive chemicals that led to the crisis and the lack of transparency around its safe disposal.
The US has phased out lead azide for munition production over the last decade due to its extreme volatility, but in doing so they moved the majority of the nation’s stockpiles to the Middletown plant, officials say. These chemicals should have been subject to regular inspections, and it is unclear how they were able to deteriorate to this extent, an issue the Iowa senator Joni Ernst alluded to in a post on X on Tuesday.
“Regarding the Army’s planned detonation in Middletown, at a time when trust in our institutions is already low, the military owes the people it serves more transparency, not less,” she said. “I expect clear leadership, real transparency, and accountability, and I will be pressing Army officials at every level for answers.”
The fallout from the Middletown detonation has underscored concerns about pollution in Iowa, an issue that became a central pillar of the 2026 midterm elections. Iowa has the second-highest rate of new cancer diagnoses in the United States and is one of only three states where overall cancer incidence is rising.
Daisy Ramirez, an Iowan who was protesting the detonation outside a separate military manufacturing plant in Rock Island, Illinois, said the operation’s proximity to farms that provide food across the US, and to the Mississippi River, whose watershed is connected to 32 states, is of particular concern. She said she and others will be pushing for both health and environmental testing after the incident to monitor the fallout.
“This isn’t just a Middletown problem, it isn’t just an Iowa problem or a midwest problem. It is a cross-nation problem,” she said.
digest_he:
תושבים באיווה, אילינוי ומיזורי מתכוננים לחג ההודיה בצילם של חששות כבדים, לקראת פיצוץ מבוקר של חומר נפץ מסוכן שתוכנן על ידי הצבא האמריקאי. המבצע נועד לנטרל 68 חביות של עופרת אזיד המאוחסנות במפעל תחמושת במידלטאון, לאחר שהתברר כי החומר הפך לבלתי יציב באופן מסוכן. הפעולה נדחתה מספר פעמים בשל לחץ ציבורי, תביעות מצד פעילים סביבתיים והתערבות פוליטית.

נציגי הצבא הסבירו כי לא נמצאה חלופה בטוחה אחרת, וכי פיצוץ מבוקר עדיף על פני פיצוץ ספונטני בלתי צפוי. עם זאת, השינויים התכופים בלוחות הזמנים יצרו בלבול רב בקרב התושבים, שקיבלו התראה קצרה בלבד לפני המועד המקורי. הרשויות המליצו לתושבים ברדיוס קרוב להתפנות, ולשאר האוכלוסייה באזור לשהות בבתים עם חלונות סגורים למשך יממה לפחות בשל סכנת אבק רעיל.

האירוע העלה שאלות קשות בנוגע לתחזוקת חומרי הנפץ והיעדר השקיפות מצד הרשויות, נושא שעורר סערה גם במערכת הבחירות האחרונה באיווה. חקלאים רבים באזור החלו לנקוט אמצעי זהירות בעצמם, כולל בדיקות קרקע והגנה על מזון לבעלי חיים, בזמן שפוליטיקאים מקומיים דורשים מענה ותשובות ברורות מהצבא.
